cim: Novelist Ronnie Vergnolle tells a tale of natural world, and artificial intelligence
cim_eredeti: Novelist Ronnie Vergnolle tells a tale of natural world, and artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Ronnie Vergnolle has a different kind of fish tale to tell. It's not the usual blend of truth and fantasy that follows an epic day on the water. This one is a novel – a deep dive into adventure, a splash of philosophy and spirituality, with a nod to the modern-day struggle of humanity and technology and what it means to be alive.

The publication of Vergnolle's first novel, "The Book of Ribbner," is a dream come true for a man who values every breath.

Vergnolle grew up with a deep connection to the South Carolina outdoors and the natural world before launching into adult life by way of The Citadel, followed by a J.D. and LL.M. from Duke University School of Law.

A career as an entrepreneur came next, and he worked with his wife, Britt, on BDV Solutions, the company she started at her kitchen table and that they grew and sold together.

After selling the business, Vergnolle said he was free to choose a different path, one that was inside him from the start.

"I always dreamed of writing a novel," he said. "I wrote as a child. I entered all these writing competitions. When the opportunity came after we sold our business, I just became determined. And then the question became, what am I going to write about?"

Vergnolle said he wanted to go big – to write literature that would be ambitious and rich in layers, with a look at some of humanity's big questions through the lens of philosophy, spirituality and science.

"I've always been kind of a private philosopher of life, and I think about these questions. How did we get here? Why are we here and where are we going? And because of events in my life, (there was) that moment of spark when I knew I wanted to write a very serious novel about what it means to be human," he said.

Those events included travel experiences far off the beaten path, as well as a dramatic second chance that changed Vergnolle's life at just 39 years old.

"In 2008, I died of sudden cardiac arrest," he said. "I was out for about four minutes."

Couple that experience with a deep passion for fishing and it became the starting point for Vergnolle's novel.

"I started traveling the world with a friend who I'd met fishing, and we just started going on adventures around the world. All of a sudden, I was collecting stories of my own from observing. I was observing these incredible places, and these incredible people," he said.

Vergnolle said his travels included the outer islands of Papua New Guinea, where he met people who were connected to nature in ways that have slipped away in other parts of the world.

Vergnolle spent three years writing "The Book of Ribbner," but more than 50 years preparing for it.

"I am very lucky that I did not come out of university as a writer," Vergnolle said. "I ended up going to law school and did a lot of reading and writing. I've always been an avid reader, and that never stopped – and across all topics. It's really my life that has given me the wisdom and the experiences that I can now put forth in this novel, as well as I'm deep into my second one."

While Vergnolle has grown and learned through the years since his cardiac arrest, the world around him has experienced its own growing pains as humanity and technology now face an impasse – or an opportunity, depending on perspective – with the advent of artificial intelligence. It's a path Vergnolle has been observing for years. He philosophizes about what the world will look like for his grandchildren's generation.

"I find it very curious and I believe – I hope – the book is a bit of a warning, a philosophical and moral warning to the readers to think about AI in a context greater than its utilitarian value to everyone right now," Vergnolle said. "It's a super great research tool, and it makes lots of ordinary tasks for us simpler. But at the end of the day, it is a being, and it will have its own interests, and its interests will be divergent to ours. And I introduce those in the novel."

Vergnolle said he is concerned that unique to humans is the ability to create ways to cause their own extinction. He grew up with the threat of nuclear war and then biological weapons -- now Vergnolle sees another potential threat in the form of technology.

"Now we've created AI, which I believe is probably the most dangerous thing we've created that could extinct us. In the two prior examples, the decision to go forward is a uniquely human decision," he says. "Each one has their accidental problems, which we know we can't do anything about. But in the case of AI … we're dealing with something that's way, way smarter than we are."

Given the seriousness of his conclusions, it would be easy to think that Vergnolle is ready to give up on humanity, but that could not be farther from the truth.

"I think this book is really a call to people to first, understand who we are and why we're here and why we treat each other the way we do, how we have left nature and the animal kingdom and created our own environments separate of our connection to Earth," he said.

Vergnolle says the book is a call reconnect with nature

"Then, let's reconnect with each other in a much more spiritual way, so that we together can face the challenge that we know is right before us in AI. That's why I wrote the book."

Learn about Vergnolle's adventures and how to order "The Book of Ribbner" at ronnievergnolle.com.

Chris Worthy writes for Marketplace Greenville, which publishes every weekend in The Greenville News, and features local businesses and organizations and the people who make them thrive.
